name: Microsoft Certified: Information Security Administrator Associate
title: Practice Exam 2
note: Microsoft scores SC-401 on a 1–1000 scale with 700 to pass. This practice exam reports a straight percentage; treat 80% as your readiness bar.

cs.title: Case Study — Adatum Corporation (Pharma Research)
cs.body:
Adatum Corporation is a pharmaceutical research company with 8,000 employees on Microsoft 365 E5.

• Scanned lab reports (PDF images from flatbed scanners) uploaded to SharePoint Online
• Proprietary drug compound names unique to Adatum — not publicly documented, no consistent alphanumeric pattern
• Most sensitive trade secret documents require encryption that no cloud provider can access
• External academic collaborators have B2B guest accounts in Adatum Teams and SharePoint
• FDA 21 CFR Part 11 compliance required for all electronic records

yn.title: Yes / No
yn.body:
Adatum configures the MPIP Scanner on Windows Server 2022 to scan on-premises network shares. A content scan job is created with Policy enforcement set to Off (Discover mode). SQL Server Express is installed on the scanner server.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true or No if it is false.

questions.stem: Adatum uploads scanned PDF lab reports to SharePoint. DLP policies must detect SSNs and compound codes in these scanned images, but detection is failing for PDF files. What must be enabled in Microsoft Purview first?
options: Advanced classification scanning in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
Document fingerprinting for PDF file formats
Optical Character Recognition (OCR) in Microsoft Purview Information Protection settings
Enhanced PDF protection in sensitivity label encryption configuration
questions.explanation: C is correct. OCR (Optical Character Recognition) must be explicitly enabled in Microsoft Purview Information Protection settings before DLP and auto-labeling policies can read text out of scanned PDFs and image files. OCR is OFF by default. Once on, OCR extracts text from images during content scanning so SITs can match against the extracted text. A is wrong because 'Advanced classification scanning in MDE' is not the gating setting for image-based content classification in Purview — Purview OCR is. B is wrong because document fingerprinting matches structural template layout, not image-to-text conversion. D is wrong because 'Enhanced PDF protection' is not a real Purview setting and would not enable image OCR even if it existed.

questions.stem: Adatum needs to detect documents containing proprietary compound names that no built-in SIT recognizes. The names follow no consistent alphanumeric pattern and cannot be enumerated in a finite list. What should they build?
options: A custom regex SIT with a pattern matching the general structure of compound names
A trainable classifier trained on example documents containing compound name content
An EDM classifier using a database table of all compound names
A keyword dictionary SIT listing all known compound names
questions.explanation: B is correct. Trainable classifiers use machine learning to recognize content categories from training examples — ideal when content has no consistent pattern and cannot be enumerated. Because Adatum's compound names have no fixed alphanumeric pattern and the full list cannot be reliably enumerated, a classifier trained on documents containing compound-name content is the strongest match. A (regex SIT) is wrong because no consistent pattern exists to write a regex for. C (EDM) is wrong because EDM requires a finite, enumerable data table — and Adatum cannot enumerate all compound names. D (keyword dictionary SIT) is wrong because it requires listing all terms; the question states the names cannot be enumerated.

questions.stem: Adatum requires that the most sensitive trade secret documents be encrypted such that Microsoft, Azure, and any cloud provider cannot decrypt them — even under legal compulsion. What encryption technology meets this requirement?
options: Azure Rights Management with Bring Your Own Key (BYOK)
Double Key Encryption (DKE)
Microsoft Purview Customer Key for M365 data at rest
Advanced Message Encryption with custom branding and access control
questions.explanation: B (DKE) is correct. DKE uses two simultaneous encryption keys: one held in Azure RMS (Microsoft) and one held exclusively by the organization on infrastructure Microsoft does not operate. Both keys are required for decryption — Microsoft cannot decrypt DKE content alone, even under legal compulsion. A (Azure RMS with BYOK) is wrong because while the customer supplies the root, Microsoft still has operational access to the key in Azure. C (Customer Key) is wrong for the same reason — Microsoft has operational access to keys in Azure Key Vault. D (Advanced Message Encryption) is wrong because AME is for emails, not document-level encryption, and Microsoft retains operational access to AME keys.

questions.stem: External academic collaborators (B2B guests) need access to SharePoint documents labeled Confidential - Research. The label uses Assign permissions now encryption scoped to internal Adatum users only. Collaborators receive Access Denied errors. What should Adatum configure?
options: Remove the encryption from the Confidential - Research label for any document shared externally with guests
Create a sublabel Confidential - Research (External) that grants access to the collaborator email domains or specific guest accounts
Grant collaborators SharePoint Site Owner permissions to bypass sensitivity label encryption restrictions
Switch the label from Assign permissions now to Let users assign permissions for all externally shared documents
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Assign permissions now' grants access ONLY to the specific users, groups, or domains explicitly defined in the label. To extend access to external academic collaborators without dropping protection on internal use, create a sublabel of Confidential - Research that explicitly grants access to the collaborator email addresses or domains. This adds a targeted encrypted variant for external sharing while keeping the internal label intact. A is wrong because removing encryption defeats the purpose of the label and exposes content to anyone with the link. C is wrong because SharePoint Site Owner permissions do NOT bypass label encryption — encryption operates at the identity layer regardless of SharePoint role. D is wrong because 'Let users assign permissions' shifts the burden to senders and creates inconsistent protection — not a sustainable enterprise pattern.

questions.stem: How do named entity SITs (such as All Full Names or All Physical Addresses) differ from standard pattern-based SITs?
options: Named entity SITs use regular expressions; standard SITs use machine learning models
Named entity SITs use machine learning models; standard SITs use rules, regex patterns, and keyword lists
Named entity SITs only detect content in English; standard SITs support multiple languages
Named entity SITs require EDM for high-confidence matching; standard SITs are self-contained
questions.explanation: B is correct. Named entity SITs (All Full Names, All Physical Addresses, Medical Terms) use machine-learning models to detect real-world entities that vary significantly in format, language, and structure — traditional regex cannot reliably capture them. Standard pattern-based SITs use regex with supporting keyword lists, ideal for structured data like credit card numbers or SSNs. A reverses the technologies — that is the opposite of how the two SIT families work. C is wrong because named entity SITs cover multiple languages, not just English. D is wrong because named entity SITs do not require EDM corroboration; they are self-contained ML detectors.

questions.stem: When must you re-upload and re-hash the sensitive data table for an EDM classifier?
options: Every 90 days — EDM hashes expire automatically on a fixed schedule
Only when the EDM schema definition (column structure) changes
Whenever the underlying database records change and you need current matching accuracy
Once per year during the annual data governance review period
questions.explanation: C is correct. EDM hashes represent the data at a specific point in time. When the underlying database records change — new hires, account updates, departures — you must re-hash and re-upload the data table for EDM to reflect the current records. There is no automatic expiration; the customer chooses the refresh cadence based on data volatility. A is wrong because hashes do not expire on a fixed 90-day schedule. B is wrong because schema changes do require re-upload but record-level changes ALSO require it — schema isn't the only trigger. D is wrong because the cadence depends on how often data changes, not an annual governance review.

questions.stem: An EDM SIT has one primary element (SSN) and two supporting elements (Last Name, Date of Birth). Which condition produces a High confidence match?
options: The SSN primary element matches the database exactly on its own
The SSN primary element matches AND at least one supporting element is present in the document
All three elements — SSN, Last Name, and Date of Birth — are found together in proximity and match the same database record
The SSN primary element matches any record in the database regardless of supporting element presence
questions.explanation: C is correct. High-confidence EDM matching requires the primary element to match AND supporting elements to also be present in close proximity, all aligned to the SAME database record. This multi-field corroboration distinguishes legitimate records from coincidental pattern hits. A is wrong because matching the primary alone yields a lower confidence level. B is wrong because at least one supporting element doesn't necessarily mean both — and high confidence requires all configured supporting elements to align. D is wrong because the primary alone is not enough for high confidence.

questions.stem: During a trainable classifier testing phase, you review candidate items and mark some as Not a match. What does this labeling provide to the classifier?
options: A positive sample confirming this content is a good example of the target category
A negative sample teaching the classifier that this content does NOT belong to the target category
A neutral sample that has no measurable impact on classifier accuracy
A false positive correction that permanently removes the item from the candidate pool
questions.explanation: B is correct. During the testing phase, items marked 'Not a match' become negative samples that teach the classifier what the target category does NOT look like — improving its ability to distinguish target content from similar-but-different content. Both positive AND negative feedback improve accuracy. A is wrong because 'Not a match' is a negative sample, not a positive confirmation. C is wrong because negative samples do measurably affect classifier accuracy. D is wrong because marking an item does not 'remove it from the candidate pool' — it labels the item for training purposes.

questions.stem: An external user with a Microsoft account receives a document labeled with Assign permissions now encryption. The label grants access to Adatum internal users only. Can the external user open the document?
options: Yes — external users with valid Microsoft accounts can always access sensitivity label encrypted content
No — Assign permissions now grants access ONLY to the specific users, groups, or domains defined in the label configuration
Yes — if the external user has guest status in Adatum Entra ID directory
No — only users in the same Entra ID tenant can decrypt any sensitivity label encrypted content
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Assign permissions now' encryption grants access ONLY to users/groups/domains explicitly defined in the label configuration. External users not in those permissions cannot decrypt the content — regardless of whether they have a Microsoft account, guest status, or any SharePoint role. Encryption enforces access at the identity layer. A is wrong because a Microsoft account alone does not grant access to encrypted content. C is wrong because guest status in the directory does not bypass label permissions. D is wrong because cross-tenant access is possible when the label explicitly grants it — the limit is the label's permission list, not the tenant boundary.

questions.stem: Your organization used Azure Information Protection (AIP) with labels defined in the Azure portal. After migrating to Microsoft Purview Information Protection, where are sensitivity labels managed?
options: Azure Portal — Information Protection blade (still active for legacy labels after migration)
Microsoft Purview compliance portal — Information Protection — Labels
Microsoft Entra ID admin center — Data classification settings
Microsoft 365 admin center — Information governance policies
questions.explanation: B is correct. After migrating from Azure Information Protection (AIP) to Microsoft Purview Information Protection, all label management moves to the Microsoft Purview compliance portal under Information Protection → Labels. The Azure portal Information Protection blade is deprecated for new work. A is wrong because the Azure blade is no longer the management surface. C is wrong because Entra ID admin center does not manage sensitivity labels. D is wrong because the M365 admin center holds tenant-level settings but not label management.

questions.stem: When should you use Double Key Encryption (DKE) rather than standard sensitivity label encryption with Azure Rights Management?
options: When you need to encrypt emails sent to external recipients who do not use Outlook
When regulatory or legal requirements mandate that no cloud provider — including Microsoft — can ever access the plaintext content
When you need to apply encryption retroactively to large volumes of existing documents at scale
When users need to access encrypted content from both Windows and macOS devices simultaneously
questions.explanation: B is correct. DKE is reserved for the most sensitive content where regulatory or contractual requirements forbid any cloud provider — including Microsoft — from ever accessing the plaintext. Standard sensitivity-label encryption uses Azure RMS, where Microsoft has operational key access. DKE adds a second organization-controlled key so no single party can decrypt. A is wrong because DKE is not designed for non-Outlook email encryption; OME is. C is wrong because DKE does not specialize in retroactive bulk encryption; auto-labeling does that. D is wrong because cross-platform access (Windows/macOS) is not what DKE addresses; standard label encryption already works across platforms.

questions.stem: What is the correct sequence to configure Adaptive Protection so that DLP policies can dynamically enforce controls based on a user's current insider risk level?
options: Configure the DLP policy first with the insider risk level condition, then enable Adaptive Protection in IRM settings
Enable Adaptive Protection in IRM global settings first; once active, add the insider risk level is condition to DLP policy rules
Enable Adaptive Protection in Compliance Manager, then link it to both IRM and DLP policies from a central dashboard
Create an adaptive scope in data lifecycle management, then reference it in both the IRM policy and DLP rule conditions
questions.explanation: B is correct. The required sequence is: (1) enable Adaptive Protection in IRM global settings — this activates risk-level assignment (Minor, Moderate, Elevated) for users in IRM policy scope; (2) once Adaptive Protection is running, the 'Insider risk level is' condition becomes available in DLP rules; (3) add the condition to DLP rules to apply tiered enforcement (e.g., Elevated = block, Moderate = block with override, Minor = audit). A is wrong because DLP cannot reference risk levels before Adaptive Protection is enabled. C is wrong because Compliance Manager does not configure Adaptive Protection. D is wrong because adaptive scopes target retention policy populations, not insider-risk-driven DLP enforcement.

questions.stem: A sensitivity label policy is scoped to the Legal department (50 users). A Finance employee who is NOT in the policy scope receives a Word document with a Confidential - Legal sensitivity label applied. What happens when the Finance employee opens the document?
options: Word blocks the Finance employee from opening the document — label policy scoping enforces content access control by department
The Finance employee can open the document and see the label, but Confidential - Legal does not appear in their sensitivity bar for applying to other documents
Word automatically adds Confidential - Legal to the Finance employee sensitivity bar when they interact with the labeled document
Word prompts the Finance employee to select a label from their own policy before they can view the document
questions.explanation: B is correct. Sensitivity label policies control which labels are AVAILABLE for users to apply — not which labels users can open. The Finance employee can open and read the labeled document normally (assuming they have SharePoint/Exchange access and decryption rights). However, Confidential - Legal will not appear in their sensitivity bar because the publishing policy isn't scoped to them — they cannot apply it themselves. A is wrong because label policy scoping does not gate read access — encryption does. C is wrong because the label is not auto-added to the Finance user's bar via interaction. D is wrong because Word does not prompt them to select a label from their policy before viewing.

questions.stem: To implement Double Key Encryption (DKE), where must the organization host its second encryption key?
options: In Azure Key Vault within the organization own Azure subscription, separate from Microsoft-managed key vaults
On a server or service hosted and controlled entirely by the organization — on-premises or in a private cloud that Microsoft does not operate
In a dedicated Microsoft Purview DKE vault provisioned through the compliance portal
Distributed across both Azure and on-premises Active Directory using a hybrid key sharing configuration
questions.explanation: B is correct. DKE requires the organization to host the second key on infrastructure that Microsoft does NOT control — typically on-premises servers, or a non-Microsoft private cloud. The organization key never lives in Azure. Microsoft holds one key in Azure RMS infrastructure; the customer holds the second on its own service. Both keys are required simultaneously for decryption, so neither party can decrypt alone. A is wrong because Azure Key Vault is Microsoft-operated infrastructure — hosting the second key in Azure defeats DKE's purpose. C is wrong because there is no 'Purview DKE vault' product. D is wrong because hybrid AD key sharing is not the DKE model; DKE is two distinct keys, not a single shared key.

questions.stem: Which built-in Microsoft Purview role allows a user to create and manage sensitivity labels and auto-labeling policies without granting access to DLP policy management, retention labels, eDiscovery cases, or Insider Risk Management?
options: Security Reader
Compliance Data Administrator
Information Protection Administrator
Records Management
questions.explanation: C is correct. The Information Protection Administrator role is scoped to creating and managing sensitivity labels, label policies, auto-labeling policies, and protection settings (including DKE and Customer Key). It does NOT grant DLP, retention, eDiscovery, or IRM access — useful for least-privilege delegation of label administration. A (Security Reader) is wrong because it is read-only across security workloads. B (Compliance Data Administrator) is wrong because it is broader than label administration. D (Records Management) is wrong because it covers retention/records, not sensitivity labels.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes Activity Explorer from Content Explorer in Microsoft Purview?
options: Activity Explorer shows current labeled items; Content Explorer shows label change event history
Content Explorer shows the current inventory of labeled items; Activity Explorer shows historical label and DLP activity events
Both tools display the same data but with different visualization formats for different audiences
Activity Explorer is specifically for IRM behavioral events; Content Explorer is exclusively for DLP rule matches
questions.explanation: B is correct. Content Explorer = current INVENTORY of labeled and sensitive items across SharePoint, Exchange, and OneDrive — what is labeled right now (snapshot). Activity Explorer = HISTORY of labeling events, DLP rule matches, and endpoint activities — what changed, when, by whom (timeline). A reverses the two — Activity Explorer is history, not current state, and Content Explorer is inventory, not change history. C is wrong because the two tools surface fundamentally different data, not the same data in different formats. D is wrong because Activity Explorer covers labeling, DLP, and endpoint events broadly, and Content Explorer covers labeled content broadly — neither is restricted to IRM or DLP alone.

questions.stem: A user applies a Highly Confidential sensitivity label to a Word document and then saves it as PDF. What happens to the sensitivity label?
options: The label is lost during PDF conversion — PDF files do not support sensitivity labels
The PDF inherits the sensitivity label and its protection settings from the Office application
The PDF retains visual markings (header, watermark) but encryption is removed for compatibility
The user must manually re-apply the label to the PDF after saving it to the new format
questions.explanation: B is correct. When a labeled Office document is saved or exported as PDF directly from Word, Excel, or PowerPoint, the sensitivity label and its protection (encryption, content marking text) transfer to the PDF. The label persists across the format conversion when Office apps perform the conversion. A is wrong because PDFs DO support sensitivity labels. C is wrong because encryption is NOT dropped on export — both visual markings and encryption carry over. D is wrong because manual re-application is unnecessary; Office handles label propagation automatically.

questions.stem: A sensitivity label has content expiration set to 60 days. A user applies the label to a document on January 1. What happens on March 2 (day 61)?
options: The label is automatically removed and the document becomes an unprotected file
The document is permanently deleted from SharePoint by the expiration policy
Users with access permissions receive an access denied error when attempting to open the document
The document enters disposition review and is sent to the designated reviewer queue
questions.explanation: C is correct. Content expiration in a sensitivity label defines how long after protection is applied users can access the content. After expiration, the Azure Rights Management service returns an access-expired/access-denied response to attempted opens. The document itself is NOT deleted — it simply can no longer be decrypted. A is wrong because the label and its encryption stay on the file; it does not become unprotected. B is wrong because expiration does not delete content from SharePoint. D is wrong because content expiration is a sensitivity-label setting, not a disposition-review workflow.

questions.stem: How does a retention label configured as Retain for 5 years, then delete differ from one configured as Retain for 5 years only when the retention period expires?
options: Both labels automatically delete covered content when the 5-year period expires
Retain then delete triggers a mandatory disposition review at period end; Retain only does not require any review
Retain then delete permanently deletes content when the period ends; Retain only applies no delete action — content simply loses its retention protection and can be deleted by users normally
Both labels require administrator action to delete content — neither label type auto-deletes without manual intervention
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Retain X years, then delete' actively schedules permanent deletion (or disposition review) at the end of the retention period. 'Retain only' protects content from user deletion DURING the period but takes NO delete action at the end — content survives and is simply no longer retention-protected. A is wrong precisely because Retain only does NOT delete at period end. B is wrong because Retain then delete does not require disposition review — it permanently deletes by default unless a review is configured. D is wrong because both labels operate without manual administrator action at period end (within their configurations).

questions.stem: Your organization requires that electronic records under FDA 21 CFR Part 11 cannot be altered or deleted for 10 years. Which retention label type satisfies this regulatory immutability requirement?
options: Regular record label with Preservation Lock applied to the parent retention policy
Regulatory record label applied directly to the electronic records
A default retention label with the delete action disabled for the 10-year period
A sensitivity label with encryption preventing modification of document content
questions.explanation: B is correct. Regulatory record labels provide permanent immutability — once applied, no user or administrator can remove the label, modify the document, or delete it before the retention period expires. This is exactly what FDA 21 CFR Part 11 immutability requirements call for. A is wrong because Regular records allow admin unlocking — Regulatory records do not. Preservation Lock prevents weakening the policy but does not make individual records permanently immutable. C is wrong because a 'delete-disabled' retention label is not an immutability primitive; users with appropriate permissions could still modify it. D is wrong because sensitivity-label encryption controls access — it does not provide record immutability.

questions.stem: You want all new documents uploaded to a specific SharePoint document library to automatically receive the Internal sensitivity label. What should you configure?
options: An auto-apply sensitivity label policy targeting that library using a KQL keyword query
A default sensitivity label in the SharePoint document library settings
A retention label with default labeling configured in the SharePoint site content type
A DLP policy with an auto-labeling action triggered for new uploads to the library
questions.explanation: B is correct. SharePoint document libraries support a default sensitivity label configuration (in library settings). Any document uploaded that does not already carry a label receives the default at upload time — directly in the library settings, separate from Purview auto-labeling policies. A (auto-apply with KQL) is wrong because that approach uses Purview auto-labeling and a content query, not a per-library default. C is wrong because retention labels are a different label family — and content type defaults are a separate, less-flexible mechanism. D is wrong because DLP does not include an auto-labeling action; DLP enforces, while labeling is configured in Information Protection.

questions.stem: A DLP rule must block external email sharing of sensitive content EXCEPT when the recipient domain is in an approved partner list. Which DLP rule element should you use to implement this exception?
options: An OR operator between the external sharing condition and the approved domain exclusion condition
An exception (unless) condition in the DLP rule that excludes emails sent to approved partner domains
A separate higher-priority DLP rule that explicitly allows sharing to approved domains
A sensitivity label exclusion in the DLP policy that marks approved-partner emails as exempt from detection
questions.explanation: B is correct. DLP rules support exception ('unless') conditions that exclude specific scenarios from triggering the rule action. Adding 'except if recipient domain is in approved-partner-domains' means the block applies ONLY when external recipients are NOT on the approved list — no need for a second rule or complex OR logic. A is wrong because an OR condition would expand the rule's matches, not narrow them. C is wrong because a separate higher-priority rule that 'allows' is awkward — DLP rules are evaluated within a policy first-match-wins, and an 'allow' rule isn't the cleanest pattern. D is wrong because there is no 'sensitivity-label exclusion' marking partner emails as exempt in DLP — exceptions belong on rule conditions.

questions.stem: A user provides a business justification and overrides a DLP Block with override action. Where is this override event recorded for compliance review?
options: In the user Entra ID audit log as a policy exception event
In Microsoft Purview DLP incident management and Activity Explorer
In an email notification automatically sent to the user manager upon override
In a SharePoint compliance list maintained by the information security team
questions.explanation: B is correct. Block-with-override events — including the user-provided justification text, user identity, timestamp, and the involved content — are logged in the Purview DLP incident management dashboard and surfaced in Activity Explorer. Compliance admins can review override patterns to spot abuse or refine policy. A is wrong because the Entra ID audit log tracks identity events, not DLP justifications. C is wrong because manager emails are not the audit-of-record (and aren't sent by default). D is wrong because there is no built-in SharePoint compliance list for DLP overrides.

questions.stem: A DLP policy is in Test mode without policy tips. Which statement accurately describes its behavior?
options: Users see policy tips; admins receive email alerts; no blocking or enforcement occurs
No user policy tips are shown and no admin alerts are generated — the policy runs completely silently
No user policy tips are shown; DLP matches ARE reported in DLP activity reports for admin review; no blocking occurs
Users see policy tips; blocking occurs on high-confidence matches only; admins receive alerts
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Test mode without policy tips' (formerly TestWithoutNotifications) runs the DLP engine in evaluation-only mode: no user policy tips, no enforcement actions, but matches ARE recorded in DLP activity reports and Activity Explorer for admin review. This lets admins assess policy impact before enabling enforcement. A is wrong because policy tips are NOT shown in this mode. B is wrong because matches ARE reported even though the policy runs without user-facing tips — it is not entirely silent. D is wrong because no blocking occurs in test mode regardless of confidence.

questions.stem: A Windows device with Endpoint DLP enabled is connected to the corporate network. A user copies a sensitive file from a local drive to a mapped network drive. Can Endpoint DLP monitor this activity?
options: No — Endpoint DLP only monitors local disk operations, not network file share paths
Yes — Endpoint DLP includes copy to network share as a monitorable and controllable activity
Yes — but only if the network drive is within the same Active Directory domain as the device
No — network drive activity requires a separate SharePoint DLP policy to detect the file movement
questions.explanation: B is correct. Endpoint DLP monitors a range of file activities on Windows devices — including 'copy or move to network share.' This lets organizations detect and restrict sensitive files being moved from devices to file shares, a common exfiltration vector. The activity can be audited, warned on, or blocked per DLP rule. A is wrong because Endpoint DLP DOES monitor network-share copy operations. C is wrong because there is no AD-domain restriction on Endpoint DLP's network-share monitoring. D is wrong because SharePoint DLP is for SharePoint Online, not for network file shares.

questions.stem: You want a retention policy to dynamically include all Microsoft 365 users in the Legal department, automatically adding new hires and removing departures. Which adaptive scope type should you use?
options: Site scope — based on SharePoint site URL patterns
User scope — based on user attributes such as Department in Entra ID
Group scope — based on M365 Group membership or group attributes
Role scope — based on administrative roles assigned in Entra ID
questions.explanation: B is correct. Adaptive scopes come in three flavors — User (targets user mailboxes/OneDrive based on Entra ID attributes like Department, Title, Country), Site (SharePoint sites based on site properties), and M365 Group (group mailboxes/SharePoint based on group attributes). A User scope with Department = Legal dynamically includes current and future Legal employees with no manual policy updates. A (Site) is wrong because the targeting unit is users in Legal, not specific SharePoint sites. C (Group) is wrong because the requirement is by department, not group membership. D (Role) is wrong because 'Role scope' targets Entra admin roles — and is not the right granularity for a department's worth of users.

questions.stem: A Microsoft Teams private channel has messages that must be retained for 5 years. Which retention policy location should you select?
options: Microsoft Teams — channel messages
Microsoft Teams — private channel messages
Exchange Online — shared mailboxes (each private channel has its own mailbox)
SharePoint Online — the private channel connected SharePoint site
questions.explanation: B is correct. Teams private channel messages have a dedicated retention location ('Teams private channel messages') separate from standard channel messages. Selecting 'Teams channel messages' does NOT cover private channels — they must be explicitly added. A is wrong because standard 'Teams channel messages' does not include private channels. C is wrong because while each private channel has its own connected mailbox, you do not target it via 'Exchange Online shared mailboxes' in retention — the dedicated private-channel location is the right path. D is wrong because the private-channel SharePoint site is a separate target for FILE retention, not message retention.

questions.stem: An eDiscovery hold is placed on a SharePoint site. A user then deletes a document from the site. Where is the document preserved and can the user retrieve it?
options: In the SharePoint recycle bin — the user can retrieve it within 93 days
In the Preservation Hold Library — it is not visible to or accessible by end users
In a legal hold container accessible to both eDiscovery managers and site collection administrators
In the eDiscovery case collection results within the Microsoft Purview portal
questions.explanation: B is correct. When a hold is placed on a SharePoint site, deleted documents are moved to the hidden Preservation Hold Library — accessible only to compliance administrators and eDiscovery managers via compliance tools. End users cannot see or self-recover from it. A is wrong because the recycle bin holds items for 93 days but is bypassed under hold — items go directly to Preservation Hold Library. C is wrong because Site Collection Administrators do not have rights to the Preservation Hold Library beyond what compliance tools provide. D is wrong because the Preservation Hold Library lives in SharePoint, not in the Purview portal — case results are a separate concept.

questions.stem: Your organization stores sensitive research data in Azure Blob Storage containers. Can Microsoft Purview Content Search search this data for eDiscovery?
options: Yes — Content Search covers all Microsoft cloud storage including Azure infrastructure services
Yes — if the Azure storage account is registered in Microsoft Purview Data Map first
No — Content Search only covers Microsoft 365 workloads: Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, and similar M365 services
Yes — when Azure Blob Storage is connected via a Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps API connector
questions.explanation: C is correct. Microsoft Purview Content Search (eDiscovery) covers only Microsoft 365 workloads — Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, OneDrive for Business, Teams, Viva Engage. Azure Blob Storage, Azure Data Lake, and other Azure infrastructure storage are NOT searchable through Content Search. A is wrong because Content Search is M365-scoped, not 'all Microsoft cloud storage.' B is wrong because registering Azure storage in Purview Data Map enables data governance discovery — not Content Search/eDiscovery. D is wrong because the MDCA API connector does not extend Content Search to Azure storage.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a retention label configured as auto-apply based on sensitive information type?
options: Users select the label from the SharePoint label menu and the auto-apply policy validates their choice
The policy automatically applies the label to matching content without user interaction; manually applied labels take precedence and are not overwritten
The policy notifies users to manually apply the label — it does not apply the label itself
The label is applied to ALL content in scope, overriding any existing retention labels already applied
questions.explanation: B is correct. Auto-apply retention label policies apply labels to matching content automatically — no user action needed. However, if a user has already manually applied a retention label, the auto-apply policy respects the existing label and does not overwrite it. Manual labels take precedence. A is wrong because auto-apply does not require user menu selection — that is the manual flow. C is wrong because auto-apply applies labels; it does not merely notify users. D is wrong because manual labels are preserved — auto-apply does not override existing labels.

questions.stem: Your tenant has Microsoft 365 E3 licenses only. What is the default retention period for unified audit log events?
options: 30 days
90 days
180 days
1 year
questions.explanation: A (90 days) is correct. Microsoft 365 E3 provides 90 days of default audit log retention. (M365 E5 or E5 Compliance increases the default to 1 year; the 10-year retention adds-on extends further.) B (180 days) is wrong — there is no 180-day default. C (1 year) is wrong — that is the E5 default, not E3. D (3 years) is wrong — no Microsoft default audit retention is 3 years; custom retention policies can hit that figure but not by default.

questions.stem: An eDiscovery Manager runs a content search and wants to export results to PST files but receives a permission error. The manager has the eDiscovery Manager role. What else is required?
options: The Global Administrator role must authorize the export operation
The Export role must be explicitly added to the eDiscovery Manager role group membership
A Microsoft 365 E5 Compliance license is required for all data export operations
Site Collection Administrator rights are required on all searched SharePoint sites
questions.explanation: B is correct. The eDiscovery Manager role alone does not grant export rights — Export is a separate, explicitly assigned role. This separation of duties ensures investigators cannot extract data without additional authorization. The Export role is added via the Permissions section in the Purview portal. A is wrong because Global Admin authorization is not the mechanism — the specific Export role is. C is wrong because licensing alone does not grant export rights; role membership does. D is wrong because Site Collection Administrator rights are not the export authorization mechanism — the Export role group is.

questions.stem: How does a DLP alert differ from an IRM (Insider Risk Management) alert?
options: DLP alerts trigger on detection of sensitive data matching a rule; IRM alerts trigger on user behavioral patterns indicating potential insider risk
DLP alerts are shown to end users via policy tips; IRM alerts are visible only to administrators
DLP alerts are generated in real time; IRM alerts are generated only during nightly scheduled risk analysis
DLP alerts can trigger only on email content; IRM alerts trigger on activities across all M365 workloads
questions.explanation: A is correct. DLP detects sensitive CONTENT — specific data types (credit cards, SSNs) in specific locations. IRM detects risky USER BEHAVIOR PATTERNS — chains of downloads, exfiltration activities, and policy violations analyzed by ML risk scoring. Both generate alerts, but for fundamentally different signal types. B is wrong because DLP policy tips and IRM admin alerts are surface-level differences, not the core distinction. C is wrong because both DLP and IRM can generate alerts in near-real-time; IRM is not limited to nightly batch. D is wrong because DLP covers Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, and endpoint; it is not email-only.

questions.stem: Which factors primarily determine a user insider risk score in IRM?
options: The user salary band, performance rating, and tenure at the organization
The volume, frequency, and type of detected indicator activities, weighted by whether the user is a Priority User
The number of DLP policy violations attributed to the user in the previous 30 days only
The sensitivity labels on content the user has accessed in SharePoint and OneDrive
questions.explanation: B is correct. IRM risk scores are calculated from detected indicator activities (downloads, USB copies, email forwards, cloud uploads, sequences), the volume and frequency of those activities, and Priority User weighting if applicable. A is wrong because salary, performance rating, and tenure are not IRM inputs. C is wrong because IRM risk is broader than DLP violations alone — many indicators contribute. D is wrong because content access metadata (which sensitivity labels a user has seen) is not a direct risk-score input.

questions.stem: An IRM Analyst is reviewing alerts and sees users as Anonymized User A and Anonymized User B. The analyst needs to see real identities. What must happen?
options: The Analyst clicks the identity to de-anonymize since they are a designated IRM reviewer
An IRM Investigator or IRM Admin must perform the de-anonymization action
A Global Administrator must approve the de-anonymization request before names are revealed
De-anonymization is not possible once anonymization is enabled in IRM global settings
questions.explanation: B is correct. When IRM anonymization is enabled, all reviewers see pseudonyms by default. Only users in the IRM Investigator or IRM Admin role group have the de-anonymize permission to reveal real identities — this role separation protects employee privacy during initial triage. IRM Analysts cannot de-anonymize on their own. A is wrong precisely because the Analyst role does not include de-anonymization rights. C is wrong because Global Admin approval is not the workflow — IRM Investigator/Admin roles control it directly. D is wrong because de-anonymization IS possible — it is just gated by role.

questions.stem: An IRM alert is reviewed and determined to be a false positive — the activity was legitimate business use. Which action should the IRM reviewer take?
options: Dismiss the alert as a false positive to remove it from the active alert queue
Escalate the alert to the IRM Investigator role for mandatory secondary review
Convert the alert to a full case and then close the case as resolved
Leave the alert open — dismissed alerts must remain visible to prevent future recurrence
questions.explanation: A is correct. Alerts confirmed as false positives or benign activity should be dismissed from the triage view — this removes them from the active queue while preserving them in the historical audit log. Alerts should be promoted to a case only when investigation and action are warranted. B is wrong because mandatory escalation for every dismissed alert would create unnecessary review work. C is wrong because converting a false positive into a case is excessive — dismiss is the correct path. D is wrong because dismissed alerts remain in the historical log for audit even after being removed from the active queue.

questions.stem: When configuring the HR Connector to import employee departure data from an HR system CSV with additional columns and non-standard date formats, what flexibility does the connector provide?
options: The CSV must exactly match Microsoft required column headers and date format — no customization is permitted
The connector field mapping configuration allows you to map your CSV columns to the required Purview IRM fields
The CSV must be converted to JSON format before the HR Connector can process it
Only departure dates in MM/DD/YYYY format are accepted — all other formats must be pre-converted externally
questions.explanation: B is correct. The HR Connector setup includes field mapping configuration — you specify which CSV column corresponds to each required field (employee email, resignation date, termination date, last working day). Extra columns are ignored. Date format configuration is also supported. A is wrong because the CSV does not have to exactly match a fixed Microsoft template. C is wrong because the CSV does not need to be converted to JSON. D is wrong because the connector accepts multiple date formats configured at setup time.

questions.stem: With Microsoft 365 E5 licensing, what is the DEFAULT unified audit log retention period without any custom audit retention policies configured?
options: 90 days
180 days
1 year
10 years
questions.explanation: C (1 year) is correct. Microsoft 365 E5 (and E5 Compliance) provides 1-year default audit log retention per licensed user. (E3 defaults to 90 days.) Custom audit retention policies can extend retention further, up to 10 years with the Audit (Premium) 10-Year Retention add-on. A (90 days) is wrong — that is the E3 default. B (180 days) is wrong — there is no Microsoft default at that figure. D (10 years) is wrong because 10-year retention is NOT a default — it requires the separate Audit (Premium) 10-Year Retention add-on license on top of E5.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT available in the DSPM for AI dashboard in Microsoft Purview?
options: Which sensitivity labels are present on content accessed by Microsoft 365 Copilot
Which users or sites are identified as oversharing content surfaced by Copilot
The specific prompt text typed by users in their Microsoft 365 Copilot interactions
Whether content accessed by Copilot was unlabeled or broadly accessible across the organization
questions.explanation: C is correct — specific prompt text is NOT available in DSPM for AI. The dashboard surfaces metadata and risk signals (label coverage, oversharing, activity volume), but raw prompt/response content is treated as user data and is not exposed in the dashboard. A is wrong because label coverage on Copilot-accessed content IS shown. B is wrong because oversharing identification IS shown. D is wrong because unlabeled and broadly accessible content surfaced by Copilot IS shown.

questions.stem: Who can review flagged communications in a Communication Compliance policy?
options: Any member of the Compliance Administrator role group in the tenant
Only users explicitly designated as reviewers when the policy was created
Any member of the eDiscovery Manager role group assigned to the policy
Any member of the Communication Compliance role group regardless of policy assignment
questions.explanation: B is correct. Communication Compliance policies have designated reviewers specified at policy creation time. Only users explicitly added as reviewers for that specific policy can access and review the flagged communications — protecting employee privacy by strictly scoping access. A is wrong because Compliance Administrators do not automatically gain review access to flagged content. C is wrong because eDiscovery Manager role does not unlock Communication Compliance review. D is wrong because the Communication Compliance role group has rights only when assigned to that specific policy.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager?
options: Enforcing DLP and retention policies across all Microsoft 365 workloads
Providing a compliance score and guided improvement actions for compliance with regulations and standards
Monitoring and alerting on insider risk behavioral activities using machine learning analytics
Managing sensitivity label configurations and deployment across the entire tenant
questions.explanation: B is correct. Compliance Manager helps organizations assess and improve compliance posture against regulations (GDPR, HIPAA, ISO 27001, NIST, etc.). It produces a compliance score based on implemented controls, maps Microsoft controls to regulatory requirements, and offers prioritized improvement actions. A is wrong because Compliance Manager does not enforce DLP/retention — those are dedicated policy solutions. C is wrong because IRM, not Compliance Manager, monitors insider-risk behaviors. D is wrong because sensitivity labels are managed in Information Protection, not Compliance Manager.

questions.stem: You run a Content Search scoped to a Microsoft 365 Group. Which content locations are included in the search?
options: Only the group Exchange Online shared mailbox
Only the group connected SharePoint site
Both the group Exchange Online shared mailbox AND the group connected SharePoint site
The group mailbox, SharePoint site, AND each member personal OneDrive for Business
questions.explanation: C is correct. Content Search against a Microsoft 365 Group includes the group's Exchange Online shared mailbox (conversations, calendar) AND the group's connected SharePoint site (files, wiki, pages). Individual member personal mailboxes and OneDrive accounts are NOT automatically included in a group-scoped search. A is wrong because both the mailbox AND SharePoint site are in scope, not just the mailbox. B is wrong for the same reason — the mailbox is also in scope. D is wrong because personal OneDrive accounts of members are not part of a group-scoped search.

questions.stem: When should you use Microsoft Purview eDiscovery (Standard or Premium) instead of a basic Content Search?
options: When you need to search content for general compliance assessment with no legal proceeding involved
When you need to place holds on content locations, manage a structured legal investigation, or use advanced analytics (Premium)
Content Search is deprecated — eDiscovery is always required for all search and discovery scenarios
When searching more than 1 TB of data exceeds the inherent limitations of Content Search
questions.explanation: B is correct. Content Search is designed for ad-hoc search and export with no hold management. eDiscovery Standard adds hold management — preserving content locations tied to a legal case. eDiscovery Premium adds custodian management, advanced analytics, review sets, predictive coding, and threading — for complex litigation. A is wrong because Content Search is fine for general compliance assessment; eDiscovery is for legal proceedings. C is wrong because Content Search is still available and supported. D is wrong because data volume is not the differentiator — feature set is (holds, custodians, analytics).

questions.stem: A complex litigation case involves 15 key individuals whose mailboxes, OneDrive accounts, and Teams content must all be preserved under legal hold and searched together as a structured investigation. Which Microsoft Purview solution supports managing these individuals as named custodians with mapped data sources?
options: Microsoft Purview Content Search with a static location list covering all 15 users
Microsoft Purview eDiscovery Standard — apply individual holds to each mailbox and OneDrive manually
Microsoft Purview eDiscovery Premium — custodian management with data source mapping and custodian-specific holds
Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management — create a case and add the 15 users as supervised subjects
questions.explanation: C is correct. eDiscovery Premium introduces custodian management — you define custodians (the key individuals), map each custodian's relevant data sources (mailbox, OneDrive, Teams, SharePoint), apply custodian-level holds in bulk, manage legal hold notifications, and track responses, all within a structured case workflow. A is wrong because Content Search lacks hold and custodian management. B is wrong because eDiscovery Standard requires manual per-location hold application without custodian-centric workflow. D is wrong because IRM is for insider-risk behavior monitoring, not litigation case management.

questions.stem: In Discover mode (Policy enforcement = Off), the scanner generates a report of files matching classification rules without applying labels or modifying any files.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Discover mode (Policy enforcement = Off) is read-only — the MPIP Scanner identifies and reports matches against configured rules without applying labels or modifying any files. This is the recommended first mode to validate results before enabling Enforce mode. No would be wrong because that would imply Discover mode modifies files, which contradicts its purpose.

questions.stem: A SQL Server instance is required for the MPIP Scanner to store its configuration database and scan job results.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. The MPIP Scanner requires a SQL Server instance (Standard or Express) to store its configuration database, scan job settings, and scan results. SQL must be installed and accessible before the scanner can be configured and registered with the Purview portal. No would be wrong because SQL is a hard prerequisite — the scanner cannot run without it.

questions.stem: The MPIP Scanner can apply sensitivity labels to files on on-premises network file shares when Policy enforcement is set to On (Enforce mode).
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. When Policy enforcement is set to On (Enforce mode), the MPIP Scanner applies sensitivity labels and protection settings to files on on-premises network file shares per the configured content scan job. In Discover mode it only reports; in Enforce mode it labels. No would be wrong because labeling is exactly what Enforce mode does.

questions.stem: The MPIP Scanner can label and apply protection to files in SharePoint Online document libraries.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. The MPIP Scanner targets ON-PREMISES environments — Windows file servers, network shares, and SharePoint Server (on-premises). SharePoint Online is covered by Microsoft Purview cloud auto-labeling policies, NOT by the MPIP Scanner. These are separate, complementary solutions for different environments. Yes would be wrong because it conflates the on-prem scanner's scope with the cloud auto-labeling product.

questions.stem: When in Enforce mode, the MPIP Scanner can apply sensitivity labels that include encryption (protection) — not just visual markings.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. In Enforce mode, the MPIP Scanner applies the full configuration of the matched sensitivity label — including encryption (Rights Management protection), content marking text, and other settings. The scanner is not limited to visual markings. No would be wrong because the Scanner does apply encryption when the matched label is configured with it.

questions.stem: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint must be deployed on the scanner server for the MPIP Scanner to function.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. The MPIP Scanner is a standalone agent communicating with the Purview portal via the Azure Information Protection service — it does NOT require Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on the scanner machine. MDE is required for Endpoint DLP on Windows clients, not for the MPIP Scanner. Yes would be wrong because it would invent a dependency that does not exist.
